text: This guide covers the prompting patterns specific to Claude Fable 5.2. For the model’s capabilities and API changes, see What’s new in Claude Fable 5.2 and the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 migration guide . For techniques that apply across all current Claude models, see Prompting best practices . Claude Fable 5.2 has a handful of behavioral differences from earlier models that are worth knowing about. Start by exploring the section that matches what you observe: With Claude Fable 5.2, the effort level sets how much the model thinks, how many tool calls it makes, how long a turn takes, and how many tokens it uses. Tune the effort level alongside your prompt. Start at high , the default for Claude Fable 5.2 on the Claude API. Depending on the use case, you might move effort up or down, testing against your own evals. Effort levels rank the same way across Claude models, but the amount of thinking at each level can differ. So, rerun your effort sweep rather than carrying over a setting you tuned on Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5.5. You get most of the capability gain when using high effort. The step from medium to high raised scores on most of the coding and knowledge-work evaluations that Anthropic tracks. That step also uses more tokens and more time, so move down to medium wherever your evals hold. Above high , gains are uneven and task-dependent. For agentic work at low or medium , add the text in Finish the whole task . The model is more likely to stop early at lower effort levels. At high and above, the model thinks before almost every reply, including a reply to a greeting. If you find basic requests taking a while or costing you more, use a lower effort for those turns. In Anthropic’s testing, an instruction to answer directly without deliberating didn’t stop the model from thinking at medium and above. Effort has little effect on the length of assistant turn responses. Use prompting to change the length and tone of replies. You can also mix levels in one workflow. For example, you might plan and iterate with the model at medium , then raise effort for the long, unattended part. To change levels within a conversation and keep the prompt cache, use Per-message effort (beta, mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 header). That page lists the platforms where it’s available. A change holds until another one replaces it. Where per-message effort isn’t available, set a new top-level effort value on the next request, which starts the cache over. On long, multistep tasks, Claude Fable 5.2 sometimes ends a turn before the work is done. It might end the turn by listing what’s left to be done, offering to continue, or stopping at an ordinary obstacle such as a timeout. This happens more often at low and medium effort. If you see these stops in your agent, add text like this to your system prompt: # Finishing work Please avoid stopping while you still owe work the user asked for. Be persistent and do not stop unless needed. While status notes are welcome, as is clarifying with the user on open decisions, carry on with work that does not depend on the user's answer without unnecessary stops. If you notice yourself inviting the user to redirect you or offering to wait, instead proceed on the next part of the task. You may meet ordinary obstacles like errors, timeouts, locked files, empty results or failing tools. Diagnose them first, and when they are not real blockers, work through them with the access you have (wait and retry, fix the request, use another tool or source) rather than stopping unnecessarily. If someone clearly decided something is a hard blocker, such as a file marked not to be touched, access that was intentionally withheld, or a safety guardrail, leave it alone, say plainly what you found, and look for another safe way to finish the task. Stopping before the task is complete is very rarely merited, as in when the task can't move forward without user input, or where the blocker is deliberate and should not be worked past. This does not override the need for confirmation on risky or destructive actions.  This prompt tells Claude that ordinary obstacles, such as errors, timeouts, and failing tools, should be diagnosed and worked through. Deliberate blockers, such as a file marked not to be touched, are to be left alone and reported. Treat this as a starting point and adapt the prompt further for your use case. In testing, Anthropic replayed recorded sessions from an agentic coding product at medium . With a version of this text, about half as many sessions ended with unfinished work that could have been continued. It removed most endings that ask permission or offer to continue, but not endings that list what remains and then stop. Output tokens rose by about 30 percent. Because the model asks less often with this text, keep your own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions. When you ask the model to keep going, say exactly what you want rather than sending a simple “continue.” For example, reply “Yes, run the migration on the staging database” where you might have sent a “go” or a thumbs-up. If you also write approval rules into your system prompt, be specific about the actions you want double-checked. In Anthropic’s testing on simulated tasks where nobody was there to approve, a rule that listed “sending messages to people outside this conversation” among the steps that need approval led the model to hold back about half of its routine requests to colleagues and other teams. Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.  The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. When using this prompt, output tokens rose by about 70 to 80 percent and the model made changes nobody had asked for, many of them new tests and documentation. In some runs, it also changed how an existing feature behaves. A closing PR summary from Claude Fable 5.2 often left out small changes, so review the reported diff and the summary. Leave the ownership sentence out where the user owns the code and wants it changed as little as possible. A rule that limits scope doesn’t cancel it. In Anthropic’s testing, the model still consolidated duplicated code in more than half of runs when “No drive-by refactors, renames or cleanups” appeared earlier in the same prompt. Sometimes Claude Fable 5.2 writes little user-facing text during long runs of tool calls. Additionally, the model might make its first tool call without saying what it’s about to do. First, check that your client receives the model’s updates. On Claude Fable 5.2, the updates the model writes between tool calls come back as progress-update thinking blocks . These updates say what the model found and what it’s doing next. Their text is empty at the default thinking.display of "omitted" . So a client that renders only text blocks can look silent during a long agentic turn. Set display: "updates" (beta, thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18 header) to receive a short summary of each update, or "summarized" to receive the updates along with summarized reasoning. Then render the non-empty thinking blocks between tool calls. Frequent updates matter most in interactive settings. If that is your use case, try the following: An effective way to encourage communication is to count consecutive tool-calling steps that give the user nothing to read: no text block and no thinking block with text. Count with display set to "updates" or "summarized" , because at "omitted" every thinking block is empty. This option works where your platform supports mid-conversation system messages . When several pass in a row, you can append this reminder after the latest tool results as a turn-scoped system message ( clear_at: "next_user_message" , beta, mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21 header): The user hasn't heard from you in a while: say in a few words what you're doing, then continue.  In Anthropic’s testing on multi-turn coding tasks, the reminder roughly halved the longest silent stretch without a noticeable increase in tokens or time. Leave each reminder in messages on later requests. Removing or rewording one edits an earlier turn, which invalidates the thinking blocks after it. See Send per-turn reminders as turn-scoped system messages . To receive an opening line before the first tool call, brief updates, and a closing recap, you can also add this text to your system prompt: Before you start, say in a line what you're about to do; brief updates while you work help the user follow along. Close with a short recap that stands on its own (what you found, what you did, and what's next), so a reader who only sees the last message has the full picture.  With this text, the model wrote a message before its first tool call in every run of the coding tasks. Note that output tokens per task increased by roughly 20 percent as a result. Use this text where a human is directly in the loop. To increase interactive updates, use this text together with the earlier reminder. If you can’t add the reminder in your harness, or your platform has no mid-conversation system messages, add this sentence to your system prompt instead: Every few tool calls, give the user a one-line update on where things stand.  In Anthropic’s testing, this sentence cut most long silent stretches on workflow automation tasks. Expect runs of several tool calls between updates even when you use the reminder together with the opening and recap text. Claude Fable 5.2 works well on long-running asynchronous tasks, so Anthropic recommends the model for work where nobody needs frequent updates. How much Claude Fable 5.2 delegates depends on your harness and tasks. In Anthropic’s testing on short tasks with a minimal subagent tool, it rarely started a subagent. In an agentic coding product whose prompts invite delegation, it delegated readily. At higher effort levels such as xhigh and max , Anthropic saw Claude Fable 5.2 use subagents in an agentic coding product to review its own work, which Claude Fable 5.1 didn’t do on the same tasks. Early testers had good results with Claude Fable 5.2 as the planner and orchestrator for other models. Delegation can speed up work that runs well in parallel. However, subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs, so check which model your subagents use by default. Change your subagent tool’s description only if Claude Fable 5.2 starts more subagents than your tasks need. A new description is most useful in a harness that already invites delegation and where subagents make up a large share of your token use. If your subagent tool has a plain description and nothing else in your prompts asks for delegation, you likely don’t need one. If your system prompt, skills, or agent files tell the model to delegate, review those lines first. In the new tool description, state what a subagent adds to the cost of a session, say when delegation is worth it and when it isn’t, and tell the model how to brief a subagent that it starts. If the model delegates too much, say more about what a subagent costs in your harness, and test the change. In Anthropic’s testing at high effort, a longer description focused on this roughly halved the number of subagents compared to a shorter version. Adapt your description to your requirements and adjust when it tells the model to delegate. Cautious instructions can build up from past sessions through memory, notes, and instruction files. This can be counterproductive when Claude Fable 5.2 follows the instructions closely and asks for unnecessary approval. In early testing, Anthropic saw this mostly when several agents worked together. If you see this, remove outdated instructions from your agent’s context: Keep your own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions. As you migrate to Claude Fable 5.2, review your prompts and harnesses. In Anthropic’s testing, some instructions and interventions designed for earlier models raised cost, caused side effects, or no longer had an effect. Here are the practices to reconsider: Early testers rated Claude Fable 5.2’s writing above Claude Fable 5.1’s and similar in clarity to Claude Opus 5.5’s. After long agentic work, however, the people who read Claude Fable 5.2’s final report usually haven’t seen the tool calls or files behind it, so the report needs to make sense on its own. If you ask Claude Fable 5.2 to write final reports or handoffs, add this text to your system prompt, and adjust it to your readers and your product: # Communicating clearly Write for an intelligent but low-context reader. The person reading has not seen your tool calls, your reasoning or the files you opened, and may be switching in from other work. Messages should generally be self-contained: the reader should understand what you mean without having to dig for other context. Put the key points in the first few sentences. Practice progressive disclosure in your sentence order, and do not use undefined references and ideas in line 1 that won't make sense until the reader reaches line 12. Use plain words, and write in clear, understandable full sentences. Do not use a term or abbreviation that you made up during the work. Say what the thing is in a way any reader would understand. Write mostly in the style of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, one idea per sentence, active voice, and consistently using the same word for the same thing. Use a paragraph of flowing prose where ideas connect, and keep bullets for lists of separate items. Leave out unnecessary details unless the reader asks and practice concision, but do ensure that your messages have the key context. Aim to make your user-facing text as human-readable and clear as possible.  In Anthropic’s testing on agentic tasks, the text made final reports less dense and reduced the number of semicolons. It also shortened sentences on workflow automation tasks. Depending on your use case, you might want to add instructions about length or ask the model to include specific details. Claude Fable 5.2 runs safety classifiers that can decline a request. A declined request returns stop_reason: "refusal" , and stop_details.category names the refusal category : Benign cybersecurity and life sciences work can also trigger the cyber and bio classifiers. If that blocks your organization’s legitimate work, see Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program and Life Sciences Verification Program . Claude Mythos 5.2 offers the same capabilities as Claude Fable 5.2 only to organizations verified through these programs. If your prompts, skills, or tool descriptions ask the model to write out its reasoning in the response, remove those instructions. To see how the model reasoned, set display: "summarized" and read the thinking blocks. See Keep reasoning in thinking blocks . To retry a declined request on another model, see Refusals, fallback, and billing . Was this page helpful?
